 * AST-guarded classification of bash commands into slice-accurate file views.
 *
 * WHY a pure module: the chain rule, the slice algebra, and every adversarial
 * guard (ADR-0033 D1/D2/D5) are pure AST predicates — unit-testable without
 * fixtures, stores, or the pi runtime. The lifecycle layer applies the result
 * to the disk re-read; this module never touches the filesystem.
 *
 * WHY unbash instead of regex: a regex cannot tell `cat f > g` (mutation)
 * from `cat f` (view), nor `cat $F` (expansion) from `cat f` (literal). The
 * typed AST makes every dangerous shape structural: redirects, heredocs,
 * substitutions, and expansions are nodes, so fail-closed is the absence of
 * a proof rather than the presence of a pattern.

*
 * WHY: (item 9) a content filter cannot fold over `LineInterval[]` — that algebra is
 * WHY: count-based over a line count, so a keep/drop stage needs the line bytes. These ops
 * WHY: carry the filter through the ordered stage array; the lifecycle layer folds them over
 * WHY: `(true line, stream text)` pairs left to right and byte-gates the recomputed output
 * WHY: against the observed stdout. Matching is literal substring, so a regex-looking
 * WHY: pattern simply fails that gate and passes through raw.
 *
 * WHY: (item 11) `sortUnique`, `uniq` and `count` are the line-SET consumers. `sortUnique`
 * WHY: (`sort -u`) dedupes by text keeping the FIRST occurrence's true line, then orders by
 * WHY: raw bytes; `uniq` collapses ADJACENT equal runs keeping each run head; `count`
 * WHY: (`wc -l`) is terminal — it consumes the whole stream and emits its length, so
 * WHY: `parseViewSegment` refuses any stage after it. The first two reorder the stream, which
 * WHY: is why the render states the order in its header while every lease keeps the true file
 * WHY: coordinate it was folded from.

*
 * `cd <literal>` (never a `-`-leading operand), `true`, `:` — the corpus-closed
 * silent set (R3). A `-`-leading operand is an option, not a directory: bash
 * consumes `cd --`/`cd -P`/`cd -L` and, with no operand left, cds to `$HOME`, so
 * taking the flag as the target would resolve a path the model never viewed.
 *
 * WHY `prefixPosition`: every statement before the terminal view of a `;` chain
 * must be silent, and the field writes that prefix `pwd` as often as `cd`.
 * `pwd` prints the working directory, so it is admitted *only* there: the
 * position proves the sequencing is deterministic, and D9 still byte-checks
 * stdout, which carries the directory line and therefore never matches the
 * slice — the lease is refused at serve time. Outside a prefix position (an
 * `&&` chain) the set stays exactly the three commands above.

*
 * `grep`/`rg` single-file search selector (spec §3.2). Strict default-deny: only the
 * allowlisted flags above survive and the shape must be exactly
 * `[flags] PATTERN [flags] FILE [flags]`. Flags are admitted at any position before `--` —
 * before the pattern, between pattern and file, and after the file — because GNU grep/rg
 * accept post-operand options and the benchmark issues them (`grep pat -i f`). A bundled
 * single-dash cluster (`-in`, `-wF`) is decomposed and EVERY letter must be admitted; the
 * value-taking `m` may only close it (`-nm 3`). The explicit-pattern `-e` is admitted in
 * three spellings — separate (`-e PAT`), attached (`-ePAT`, handled before cluster
 * decomposition since `PAT` letters are not admitted), and cluster-close (`-ine PAT`,
 * mirroring `m`: must close, consumes the next argument) — exactly once; its value becomes
 * THE pattern so the operands must then be exactly `[FILE]`. `--` ends flag parsing, so
 * `grep pat -- -n` names the file `-n`. Fail closed: attached short values (`-m3`, `-nm3`),
 * any digit in a cluster (`-n5`), an unknown letter (`-inQ`), every `=`-long form but
 * `--max-count=N` (`--line-number=x`, `--color=always`), a value that is not a strictly
 * positive integer or not exactly `never`, `-f` (stays denied: file-input patterns break
 * the single-`PATTERN FILE` geometry), `-e` with no value, `-e` twice, a pattern both via
 * `-e` and positionally, a `-`-leading pattern with no `--` (unless given via `-e`), zero
 * operands (stdin), and more than `BASH_SEARCH_MAX_FILES` file operands.
 * Globs, tildes and expansions never reach here because `stageShape`/`literalValue` reject
 * them first.
 * WHY: (item 10) the operand arity now spans four shapes — `[PATTERN FILE]` (single-file),
 * WHY: `[PATTERN FILE...]` (multi-file), `grep -r PATTERN DIR` (recursive walk) and
 * WHY: `rg --files [DIR]` (anchorless list). Their stdout geometries differ (`LINE:content`,
 * WHY: `FILE:LINE:content`, a path list), so the family is returned as a tagged union rather
 * WHY: than one widened interface. Directory operands are still NOT detected here: this module
 * WHY: is pure and zero-fs, so the lifecycle layer re-checks the resolved file kind — and
 * WHY: upgrades an `rg` directory operand (rg recurses by default) while a `grep` directory
 * WHY: operand stays raw (native grep errors without `-r`).

*
 * Bash conversion as data (ADR: #151): the `classifyBash` guard chain, transcribed rule by rule
 * into one ordered table instead of an inline `if` ladder.
 *
 * WHY a table: array order is precedence — a new rule is inserted at its altitude and every guard
 * it can shadow is visible above it, which is exactly what the inline chain made expensive
 * (the #135 gate and the declined compounds both turned on shadowing). Each rule cites the source
 * line it was transcribed from (pre-extraction `src/bash-classifier.ts`) and the ADR it implements.
 *
 * WHY the phases: the chain has loop-carried state (statements feed segments feed blocks), so a
 * flat pass cannot express it. `decide` runs each phase's entries in array order — pre, then one
 * statement walk (guards plus the structural segment push), then the chain ceiling, then one
 * segment walk, then the conversion tail. Inside a walk, `run` returns `ADVANCE` to move to the
 * next statement/segment (the transcribed `continue`) or a `Decision` to stop; `undefined` from
 * `fireRule` means no rule fired. Accumulation (glue admission, `cd` recording, block recording)
 * lives inside the entries because the source interleaves it with the guards.
 *
 * Scope note: `Decision` mirrors the established `BashClass` union (including the `passThrough`
 * kind spelling) rather than inventing new block types — S1 is zero behaviour change, and the
 * serve seams already switch on those kinds.

*
 * `bash.multiFile` — the multi-file view caps (ADR-0049 M6), the sibling of `bash.view`.
 *
 * WHY the caps are settings: they are operator policy over how much one bash result may spend, not
 * a correctness bound (the ADR's safety bound IS the allowed range — a config can only lower a cap,
 * never raise it past the hard maximum). They resolve per KEY through the shared project/global
 * ladder so "the project file is set" never stands in for "this key came from the project file".
 *
 * WHY an out-of-range value warns instead of falling through silently: ADR-0049 M6 requires the
 * warning, and a dropped cap changes how much the session serves — the silent drop this ladder
 * refuses to make at file level is the same drop one level down. A MISSING key still warns about
 * nothing, and a broken file keeps warning exactly once through `readScopeConfig`.
 *
 * This module never touches the filesystem itself: reads go through `readScopeConfig`, writes
 * through `updateConfigFile`, so the config file keeps one owner.

*
 * Bash view setting — the `bash.view` key of the shared config file, resolved
 * through the shared ladder: env override, then project file, then global file,
 * then the default.
 *
 * WHY the interception is configurable at all: the view replacement swaps bash
 * stdout for anchored lines, which is a display decision about the model's own
 * session — an operator who would rather see raw output turns one key off, and
 * every other session keeps the default without restating it.
 *
 * WHY a warning is part of the contract here: a dropped setting changes what the
 * session shows, so an existing-but-unusable file is reported through `onWarn`
 * while the value falls through the ladder. A missing file warns about nothing,
 * and a value outside the accepted shape is ignored exactly as the sibling
 * ladders ignore one. Nothing here throws on the read side.

*
 * The retired per-user config directories, strongest first: each one held the settings file AND
 * every state artifact before #190, which is exactly the coupling this relocation breaks. Read once
 * for adoption, never written again.
 *
 * WHY the override comes first: a user who set `PI_BETTER_EDIT_CONFIG_DIR` before the relocation
 * kept `pi-better-edit.json`, `hash-store.json` and the logs directly in that directory, and the
 * override is still the strongest statement about where that user meant their files to live.
 *
 * WHY the XDG base is read HERE and only here: the pre-#190 ladder honoured `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME`, so a
 * user who relocated the old directory through it has their settings and state under that base.
 * Adoption is the one job that has to look where the old ladder looked — every NEW path is derived
 * from the agent dir and the state home, so changing this variable never moves a file written by
 * this version. A relative value is ignored, as it was.
 *
 * WHY deduped: an unset `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME` resolves to `<home>/.config`, so two rungs collapse into
 * one and a single artifact must not be visited, moved or reported twice.

*
 * The two directories this extension owns, and the only module that names any of their paths.
 *
 * WHY two roots rather than one: settings belong to the pi agent tree (an operator reads them
 * beside the other extensions they configure), while the store, the legacy JSON and the
 * diagnostics log are STATE — machine-written, disposable, and never edited by hand. The XDG
 * state directory is where a machine-written artifact belongs, and keeping settings out of it is
 * what stops a `rm -rf` of the state root from deleting the user's configuration.
 *
 * WHY this is its own module rather than a corner of `hash-store.ts`: the diagnostics sink has to
 * answer "where is my directory?" on its very first line, and `hash-store.ts` is one of its
 * callers. Importing the directory rule from the store made a cycle (diagnostics → hash-store →
 * hash-identity → diagnostics) whose partial initialisation reached the schema as `undefined`
 * columns. The directory rule has no dependency on the store, so it lives where nothing forces a
 * cycle: below both of them.
 *
 * WHY every RETIRED path is spelled here too: `test/arch/config-ladder-single-owner.test.ts` pins
 * exactly one module naming the config-file locations. A second copy of a retired literal is how
 * an adoption chain silently reads a path nobody meant it to.

*
 * (ticket-04b section 2) Next-run repair for the foreign-cut transaction. NO filesystem atomicity
 * is claimed: the two renames leave a real window, and a crash inside it is resolved here — on
 * the NEXT run, from the durable intent record plus the correlated undo rows — with no content
 * lost in either resolution:
 *
 * FORWARD intent (a cut that crashed between its renames):
 *  - target at POST  → the crash landed the insert but not the destructive retirement: COMPLETE
 *    the cut by writing each still-PRE member its undo row's post bytes.
 *  - target at PRE   → the insert never committed: RESTORE by writing each POST member its undo
 *    row's pre bytes (the target at PRE is the undo already; the inverse ordering is
 *    unreachable by construction and collapses to a no-op here).
 *  - every member PRE or POST with a definitive state → that state decides (all-POST merely
 *    drops the intent — the crash hit the final intent-delete).
 *  - ANY member outside both (modified or missing) → touch nothing, keep the intent: repairing
 *    over an outside write would destroy content, and the intent keeps the question open.
 *
 * REVERT intent (04b-rem P2-1: a correlated UNDO whose writes failed partway):
 *  - members at POST are not yet reverted → complete the revert by writing them their pre
 *    bytes; members already at PRE stay.
 *  - every member at PRE → the revert landed: clear the transaction's undo rows and the intent.
 *  - ANY member outside both → touch nothing, keep both: same fail-closed rule as forward.
 *
 * (04b-rem P2-2) The state oracle compares BYTES, never decoded text: the abort/rollback arms
 * rest members at their RAW pre-images (never canonically folded), so a mixed-line-ending
 * member must be recognized from its raw bytes — a text oracle would read it as "other" and
 * the intent would leak forever. The rows carry the raw pre image precisely for this reason.
 *
 * Store materialization is deliberately byte-only: the next read re-materializes snapshots and
 * leases from the committed bytes (the repo's deferred-sync semantics), so repair can never
 * half-write the store.

*
 * The extension's ONLY diagnostic sink.
 *
 * WHY this exists at all: the extension runs inside Pi's process, and that process owns the
 * terminal through a differential renderer (`pi-tui` main screen): it tracks the hardware cursor
 * row and the lines it last painted, and repaints only what it believes changed. A write to
 * stdout/stderr therefore lands at whatever cursor position the frame happens to occupy — the text
 * is splatted across unrelated rows, interleaved with the UI, and erased by the next paint. It is
 * also uncopyable: by the time a selection starts, the renderer has rewritten the cells. That is
 * exactly how `console.error("Bash view interception failed:", error)` surfaced: a stack trace
 * smeared over the view, gone when you tried to select it.
 *
 * WHY the file lives in `stateRoot()` and nowhere else: the log is STATE — machine-written,
 * disposable, rotated by size — and the state root is the one base directory this extension writes
 * at runtime (the store, its WAL, the janitor's bookkeeping and the pre-SQLite JSON store). ONE
 * rule: `<stateRoot>/diagnostics.log`, rotated to `<stateRoot>/diagnostics.log.1`. The operator's
 * `PI_BETTER_EDIT_CONFIG_DIR` still moves it, through `<override>/state/`; settings deliberately do
 * NOT share this directory, so clearing state never deletes configuration.
 *
 * WHY JSONL and not prose: the records carry stack traces, and a stack trace in prose needs either
 * multi-line records (unparseable) or escaped newlines (unreadable). One JSON object per line is
 * both — `jq -r '.error.stack[]'` prints a normal trace, `grep` still finds a line by message.
 *
 * WHY synchronous appends: a record is written at most once per failure, and a synchronous append
 * keeps records ordered and never floats a promise that an exit could drop. The cost is paid on
 * failure paths only, never on the happy path.
 *
 * WHY nothing here may throw: this is the last resort of a best-effort hook. A diagnostic sink that
 * can fail its caller turns "the view passed through" into "the tool call errored" — the very
 * failure it exists to make visible. Every entry point swallows its own I/O errors.

*
 * Domain error registry — the closed, type-safe contract for every
 * negative-path rejection (spec docs/spec/unified-error-and-warning-contract.md
 * section 4, D1). Its only import is the dependency-free alphabet leaf
 * (`./hashline/alphabet.js`, which itself imports nothing), so any seam can
 * still throw without wiring a store, session, or hasher.
 *
 * INVARIANT (the point of this module): a code is never declared without a
 * producer. Every `DomainErrorCode` member must have at least one
 * `new DomainError(code, payload)` site in src/, and every code passed at a
 * throw site must be a union member. Asserted BOTH directions in
 * test/arch/domain-error-registry.test.ts. This is what makes the registry a
 * contract instead of a list.
 *
 * WHY: payload text reports facts. A served `Options:` section may appear only
 * when it is neutral, unharmful and fail-closed, AND the evidence pins a single
 * cause. Neutral means an explicit list of admissible next moves that keeps the
 * model's choice — never one directive, because a biased suggestion steers the
 * model's next action. A code with no neutral option declares none and renders
 * facts only.
 *
 * WHY: options live on the refusal, never in a prompt or on a success path. They
 * render only for `MODEL` audience. `E_LARGE_FILE` stays fact-only until its
 * payload can name the invoking tool, because read and edit need different
 * options. `E_SUSPICIOUS_TEXT` is the reference: two options, and the payload
 * arm selects text vs content.
 *
 * See ADR-0047.

*
 * WHY (CAND-9, ADR-0023): the drift-notice episode identity is the drifted line's rebased
 * position in the CURRENT file — not its anchor string. An anchor is a spelling, not an
 * identity: one reported entry for a hash shared by two distinct lines silenced both
 * (duplicate-hash collapse), and a lease rotation renamed the mirror anchor of an
 * already-reported line, spuriously re-noticing it. The session's reported-set keeps storing
 * strings (schema unchanged); this base-62 encoding of the position at the configured width is the KEY VALUE.
 * Positions are bounded by `SERVED_MAX_LINES` (the served admission budget), which
 * already sits below the anchor-space ceiling, so the encoding is injective over
 * every reachable position.
 * An out-of-file position (never shown, never marked) keys on "" — not a valid stored entry, always
 * "not yet reported", matching the legacy behavior for unshown drift.

 * SAFETY: edit-diff - row-intrinsic invisible-code-point annotation (issue #231).
 *
 * WHY: in-scope code points are a vanishingly small share of real-corpus characters,
 * WHY: so fatigue is not the risk; a missed disclosure is a silent byte change. The
 * WHY: annotation therefore lives on the diff rows themselves instead of a sentence:
 * WHY: each `-` row lists its own in-scope code points as `removed`, each `+` row
 * WHY: lists its own as `added`, in column order on one sub-row placed immediately
 * WHY: after its row. There is no cross-row pairing and no aggregation - block
 * WHY: rewrites annotate both sides independently - and context rows never get
 * WHY: sub-rows. The sub-row carries no file-line slot: adjacency to its diff row,
 * WHY: whose anchors map to the file line, carries the line.

*
 * genDiff is the single diff projection (#169). Return contract:
 * - every emitted row's anchor equals the true new-file line content hash at that
 *   position; removed rows carry the true old-file hash when old hashes are provided.
 * - every emitted marker's count equals the span it hides:
 *   ` ... [N lines untouched] ...` advances both cursors past N hidden rows, keeping every FOLLOWING
 *   emitted anchor at its true file position; whether the hidden rows are addressable is a property
 *   of the serve that carries this projection (rows rendered through serve paths are leased there),
 *   not of this renderer, and ` - ... [N lines deleted] ...` advances the old cursor past
 *   N deleted rows (cursor-exact).
 * - collapse invariant: a middle gap smaller than 2×context renders whole (#166/#172);
 *   at context 0 every non-empty middle gap collapses to a single counted untouched
 *   marker (#170); bare ` ...` appears only at leading/trailing edges; added spans are never collapsed.
 * - servedRows mirror exactly the rendered context/addition rows (position + hash).
 * - `firstChangedLine`/`lastChangedLine` bracket the changed new-content lines (1-indexed,
 *   `lastChangedLine >= firstChangedLine` whenever either is set); a pure deletion names the
 *   position where the removed text sat, so an end-of-file deletion may name one line past the
 *   last new line — exactly as `firstChangedLine` already can, and both are absent on a no-op.

*
 * Wraps MULTIPLE rejected items of a multi-item call for the model. Sibling of `batchAbortFor`:
 * one aggregated rejection with one bullet per failing item (`- edit[1]: …`) so a single
 * resubmission can fix them all instead of burning one turn per failure. The batch is still
 * all-or-nothing — the atomicity trailer is identical — and each item keeps its own diagnostic
 * (and code) inline, so the model can act on every failure without a re-read.
 *
 * Field aggregation (spec D2 — the envelope must stay actionable):
 * - `code`: every item keeps its own `[E_*]` inline in the message; the envelope carries the
 *   first item's domain code so `toFailure` still routes the typed path (and keeps this full
 *   message) instead of rewriting it as `E_UNKNOWN`.
 * - `details`/`cause`: carried only when every failing item agrees on one diagnosis; a mixed
 *   batch states each cause inline instead of promoting one.
 * - `servedRows`: the union of every failing item's rows (each item's retry leases were already
 *   recorded on its own rejection path).
 * - `servedBlock`: every failing item's block, in item order.

 * SAFETY: single owner of the rejection envelope. The five forwarded fields are `code`,
 * `details.cause`, `servedRows`, `servedBlock`, and `payloadMessage`. Every rejection carries
 * them from its producer to the engine's reader. Before this module each site
 * hand-copied them through `as { code?: string }` casts (batch-abort wrappers,
 * the tool-seam throw, `toFailure`'s sniff), so adding a field meant five edits.
 *
 * Design (chosen over an Error subclass): the wire shape stays plain properties
 * on the caught `Error`, and this module owns BOTH ends — `attachEnvelope` (the
 * only writer) and `readEnvelope` (the only reader/validation seam). A subclass
 * would force `DomainError` — whose public surface the registry tests pin — or
 * the batch wrappers onto a new hierarchy without deepening anything: the
 * wrappers must stay `instanceof Error`-plain while a caught `DomainError` is
 * still routed by class identity in `toFailure`. Adding a sixth envelope field
 * `readEnvelope` — never a call-site change.
 *
 * Honesty rule: the read validates, it does not trust. Only a registry member
 * survives in `code` and only a `RangeCause` member in `cause` — errno-style
 * pass-through is not a legitimate use: `toFailure` already routes non-registry
 * codes to `E_UNKNOWN`, so a dropped field changes no routing decision. The
 * writer keeps the `details: { code?, cause }` projection in lockstep with the
 * top-level `cause`, preserving the engine's failure shape; registry-typed
 * fields are forwarded unchanged, while untyped extras on `details` are no
 * longer carried (no in-repo consumer reads them).

 *
 * WHY a header read replaces the full `PRAGMA quick_check` here: the stamp gate removed the sweep,
 * so the integrity sweep became the dominant remaining cost of a stamp-matching open — it walks
 * every page of the store — and what it buys is EARLIER notice, not prevention. The remedy for a
 * damaged store is `quarantineStore` plus a rebuild from empty, because this store is a
 * disposable CACHE: the served mirror, the snapshots and their lineage are all re-derived from the
 * files on disk on the next read. Paying the dominant share of every process's open latency, on
 * every open, to move that notice a few statements earlier was the bad trade.
 *
 * WHAT IS DELIBERATELY NOT CHECKED, and where the check MOVES to instead: page-level damage inside
 * an otherwise well-formed file — a torn b-tree page, a freelist that disagrees with itself — is
 * not visible from the header. Such corruption surfaces LATER, at the statement that first touches
 * the damaged page, as its own error (`database disk image is malformed`, SQLITE_CORRUPT), never
 * as a silently wrong result: every honoring path re-derives from the bytes it is about (see the
 * trap-(c) block above). Issue #90 INHERITS the throttled deep check: its janitor sweep runs the
 * store's own maintenance off the tool-call path, so the deep pass is MOVED rather than lost.

*
 * The HEAL half of the janitor's periodic deep check: when the open store fails `isHealthy`, quarantine
 * and rebuild as the open path's own recovery does — through the one `quarantineStore`, then
 * `openStore` — and report whether that happened. Called only by the store janitor
 * (`src/store-janitor.ts`), off the tool-call path.
 *
 * WHY it re-checks instead of trusting its caller's verdict: this is then safe to call from
 * anywhere and can never quarantine a healthy store, which is the property the open path's own
 * recovery has too (`if (... !isHealthy(db))`). The cost is one extra `PRAGMA quick_check` on a
 * store already known to be damaged.

 * `shutdownHashStore`, then `quarantineStore`, then `openStore` — and every piece of state it drops
 * is re-derivable, because the store is a disposable cache: the served mirror, the snapshots and
 * their lineage are all rebuilt from the files on disk. What it does NOT

*
 * The SQLite database header — the 100-byte prefix of every database file, described by the file
 * format spec (`fileformat2.html` §1.3, "The Database Header"). Every field below is read from
 * those bytes directly, which is what makes the smoke check cheap: no page cache, no statement, no
 * lock — one read of the file's first page.
 *
 * WHAT EACH FIELD CARRIES, and the range this check holds it to:
 * - bytes 0-15: the magic string `SQLite format 3\000`. A file without it is not a database.
 * - bytes 16-17: the page size, big-endian, a power of two from 512 to 32768 inclusive — or the
 *   literal value 1, the format's encoding of 65536.
 * - bytes 28-31: the database size in pages, big-endian. The main file's page count only: WAL
 *   frames live outside it (measured — the field equals the file's own page count both while a WAL
 *   is pending and after a checkpoint, on the same store). Zero means "size unknown" to SQLite,
 *   which then derives the size from the file; no open of this store writes zero, so this check
 *   reads it as damage instead of guessing.
 * - the file's length must then be exactly page size x page count.

*
 * SAFETY: Edit-path lease resolution — the MVCC identity seam for `edit` (spec §3.1.1, §3.5).
 *
 * Two lease paths, chosen by ONE predicate, verified by ONE gate:
 *
 *  - **Fast path** (`S_from === C ∧ S_to === C ∧ S_from === S_to`): the anchors were leased from
 *    the content now on disk, so the caller keeps applying at the served coordinates.
 *  - **Dynamic rebase path**: the caller resolved each leased `line_id` in `line_lineage(C)` (an
 *    on-demand materialization through `pairSnapshots`) and applies at the rebased coordinate.
 *
 * Both paths run `verifyRebasedSpan` over the whole served window (#151, spec §3.5): the fast path
 * is the rigid remap whose rebased coordinates happen to equal the served ones, so per-line lease
 * identity and retirement are checked identically either way.
 *
 * Resolution is strictly READ-ONLY on `served_leases`: it never re-stamps `line_id` and never
 * writes `retired_at`. The authoritative retirement update belongs to materialization.
 *
 * Fail-closed semantics (never weakened): an unleased anchor, a retired/absent leased `line_id`, a
 * coordinate that no longer carries the leased identity, or an external insert/delete strictly
 * inside the span all reject before any write, so a rejection leaves the file byte-identical.
 * A retired identity whose named window collapses or misses the file rejects with no rows;
 * the surviving-bound-live-and-unshifted case serves the named window as a fresh read
 * (no retry hint) with the rows leased as today; any other retired identity with an
 * identifiable window rejects with that window served for a retry.
 *
 * INVARIANT (spec §3.1.1, §5.3, ADR-0016) — a served anchor is never resolved by content. `apply.ts`
 * routes EVERY edit that has a lease source here, so a boundary anchor either has a live lease or its
 * identity is lost: a missing lease is an unknown or foreign anchor (the session-wide lookup
 * decides which), a retired identity with no live unshifted survivor and no identifiable window
 * carries no rows, and the one-bound-retired survivor-live-and-unshifted case serves a fresh
 * read to decide from, never a content question.
 * An unread (never-served) interior line strictly between the anchors is accepted (ADR-0024): it
 * carries no identity to verify, and the boundary leases plus the window-length gate pin the span;
 * a never-served BOUNDARY row keeps the fail-closed diagnosis (`[E_STALE_RANGE]`, spec §5.3).

*
 * Bounded leaf alignment (spec §3.4.4). Uniqueness is **embedding-level**: a pairing survives
 * only when it lies on every maximal traceback path, and an interval with more than one maximum
 * pairing pairs nothing (its lines stay UNPAIRED / RETIRED).
 *
 * `pairingCount` is the exact number of maximum pairings (embeddings) of the optimal LCS in the
 * sub-interval, capped at 2 so the decision stays polynomial. It deliberately counts neither
 * distinct canon strings nor DP orderings:
 * - A repeated canon that can be matched in two places counts twice, although the LCS string is
 *   the same: `[A, A, A]` vs `[A, A]` counts 3, not 1.
 * - Two orderings of down/right skips around the same matched lines count once, because they are
 *   the same embedding: `[A, X, B]` vs `[A, Y, B]` counts 1, not 2.
 *
 * The recurrence is a first-pair decomposition. For the region starting at `(i, j)` with optimal
 * length `target`, every maximum pairing either matches `i` with `j` (only possible when the
 * canons agree, and then it extends a maximum pairing of `(i + 1, j + 1)`), or leaves at least
 * one of the two lines unmatched, which is a maximum pairing of `(i + 1, j)` and/or `(i, j + 1)`
 * at the same length. The overlap of those two jump regions is subtracted, so each pairing is
 * counted exactly once. The cap is applied after the inclusion-exclusion subtraction, and because
 * `|A ∪ B| == 1` forces `A` and `B` to be the same singleton, the `=== 1` test that drives
 * `isUnique` stays exact under the cap.

*
 * Scaled recursive patience pairing (spec §5.2): aligns a previous snapshot's lines to the
 * current snapshot's lines so `line_id`s survive reorders, inserts, and deletes.
 *
 * The engine has four phases, all fail-closed: an ambiguous interval pairs nothing rather
 * than guessing coordinates.
 *
 *   1. Locally unique canon anchors become candidate pins (`findUniquePins`).
 *   2. The candidate pins' minimal-displacement LIS backbone is their unconditional
 *      intersection across every maximum-length, minimum-Δ subsequence
 *      (`findStablePinBackbone`, two-pass DP over patience-sorted ranks).
 *   3. Pinless rigid runs with identical canon sequences zip pairwise (Probe N).
 *   4. Bounded leaf intervals align on a unique LCS embedding only: a pairing is emitted when
 *      it lies on every maximal traceback path, so an interval with several optimal pairings
 *      stays UNPAIRED / RETIRED.
 *
 * When the backbone is empty the interval falls straight through to leaf handling: the
 * engine never recurses on identical bounds, so alignment cannot starve the scan budget.
 *
 * Invariant: `prevLines` and `currLines` are contiguous ascending 1-based line numbers
 * (spec §5.2 descriptor shape), so a descriptor's index + 1 is its line number.
